questions.stem: After executing a `lookup_order` call, the developer's loop sends the next request to the API with only the model's previous assistant message appended. The model then calls `lookup_order` again with the same arguments. What is wrong?

options.text: The loop doesn't append a `tool_result` block (matching the `tool_use_id`) in a user message, so the model never sees the tool's output.
options.why: Every tool call's result must go back into the conversation history.

options.text: The model needs `tool_choice: "none"` after the first call.
options.why: That would prevent all further tool use, which isn't the fix.

options.text: `lookup_order` should be called in parallel with `get_customer`.
options.why: Parallelism doesn't explain the repeated call.

options.text: The system prompt should say "don't repeat tool calls".
options.why: This treats the symptom. The model lacks the result.

questions.explanation: An agentic loop executes the requested tools, appends the `tool_result` blocks to history, and calls the model again. Missing results cause repeated or hallucinated calls.

questions.stem: Which TWO business rules in this scenario should be enforced programmatically rather than by prompt instructions? (Select TWO.)

options.text: No refund may be processed until `get_customer` has returned a verified identity.
options.why: This is a hard compliance rule that must hold every time, so it needs a programmatic gate.

options.text: Refunds above $500 require human approval.
options.why: This is a financial control that should be enforced deterministically, for example with an interception hook.

options.text: Responses should be friendly and concise.
options.why: This is tone guidance, which prompts handle well.

options.text: Mention the loyalty programme when it is relevant.
options.why: This is a soft behaviour that suits a prompt.

options.text: Use the customer's first name in greetings.
options.why: This is a style preference.

questions.explanation: Use code (hooks, prerequisite gates) for rules with compliance or financial consequences. Use prompts for style and soft guidance.

questions.stem: A PreToolUse hook blocks `process_refund` for unverified customers. When it blocks a call, what should the hook return to the agent?

options.text: A clear, structured reason (for example "blocked: customer not verified; call get_customer first"), so the agent can recover by taking the correct next step.
options.why: An informative denial lets the agent self-correct within the conversation.

options.text: Nothing. The call should silently do nothing.
options.why: Silent failure leaves the agent believing the refund succeeded.

options.text: A fake success response, to avoid confusing the customer.
options.why: Masking a block as success is dangerous.

options.text: Terminate the whole session.
options.why: This is disproportionate and recoverable.

questions.explanation: Interception hooks should block deterministically and explain why, so that the agent can redirect, for example to verification or escalation.

questions.stem: The team considers replacing the agent with a fixed decision tree (if "refund" in message → ask order ID → lookup → refund). Why is the agentic design generally preferred for this use case, and where does deterministic logic still belong?

options.text: Customer messages vary too much for fixed trees, so the model should choose the next step dynamically from tool results. Deterministic code still belongs at the policy boundaries (verification gates, refund caps).
options.why: Model-driven flow plus programmatic guardrails is the intended hybrid.

options.text: Decision trees are always better because they are deterministic, so the agent should be dropped.
options.why: Rigid trees fail on varied, multi-concern conversations and hurt resolution rates.

options.text: The agent should decide everything, including policy enforcement, so no code is needed.
options.why: Critical rules need deterministic enforcement.

options.text: Use the decision tree for refunds and let the agent handle only greetings.
options.why: This wastes the agent's value.

questions.explanation: Agentic loops let the model decide which tool to call next, rather than following a fixed tree, while hooks and gates enforce the non-negotiable rules.

questions.stem: The agent sometimes answers a question about order status from memory, without calling `lookup_order`. The developer sets `tool_choice: {"type": "any"}` for every turn. What is the side effect?

options.text: The model must call some tool on every turn, so it can never reply to the customer with plain text. That breaks normal conversation. Better tool descriptions and instructions are the right fix.
options.why: `any` forces a tool call on every turn.

options.text: There is no side effect. `any` only applies when a tool is relevant.
options.why: That describes `auto`.

options.text: It forces `lookup_order` specifically.
options.why: Forcing a specific tool requires the named form.

options.text: It disables parallel tool calls.
options.why: That isn't what `any` does.

questions.explanation: `auto`: the model decides. `any`: it must call some tool. A named tool: it must call that tool. Forcing tool use globally prevents text replies.

questions.stem: A customer asks for a refund on a custom-engraved item. The refund policy doesn't mention personalised goods. What should the agent do?

options.text: Treat this as a policy gap: explain that this case needs review, and escalate to a human with a structured summary rather than improvising a decision.
options.why: Policy gaps and exceptions are escalation triggers.

options.text: Apply the standard refund policy, since nothing forbids it.
options.why: This improvises policy on an unaddressed case.

options.text: Deny the refund, since it isn't explicitly covered.
options.why: This also improvises, and harms the customer.

options.text: Ask the customer what they think is fair and do that.
options.why: That isn't a defensible policy decision.

questions.explanation: Escalate when a case falls outside the documented policy, rather than inventing policy.

questions.stem: Two search subagents, assigned "EV charging pricing" and "EV charging business models", return largely overlapping sources and findings, which wastes budget. What should the coordinator do differently?

options.text: Partition the scope explicitly when delegating: give each subagent distinct boundaries (for example pricing data only vs. revenue models only, with exclusions) so their work doesn't overlap.
options.why: Explicit scope partitioning avoids duplicated work.

options.text: Let the synthesis agent deduplicate afterwards.
options.why: The budget is already spent. This treats the symptom.

options.text: Merge them into a single subagent.
options.why: This loses parallelism and focus.

options.text: Give both subagents fewer search results.
options.why: They would still overlap, just with less data.

questions.explanation: The coordinator should partition subagent scopes to avoid duplication and gaps.

questions.stem: Briefs often have thin sections that need more evidence. Which coordinator behaviour best improves completeness?

options.text: An iterative refinement loop: after aggregating results, the coordinator evaluates coverage against the quality criteria and delegates targeted follow-up queries for the gaps before handing off to synthesis.
options.why: The coordinator evaluates, finds gaps and re-delegates.

options.text: Always run each subagent twice and merge the results.
options.why: This is blind duplication and doesn't target the gaps.

options.text: Ask the report agent to pad thin sections.
options.why: Padding without evidence lowers quality.

options.text: Accept thin sections as a limitation.
options.why: This misses a cheap improvement.

questions.explanation: Coordinators can run iterative refinement loops: evaluate output against the criteria, then delegate follow-ups.

questions.stem: The team wants a reusable "fact-checker" subagent with its own instructions and a restricted toolset (fetch only, no search). How should it be defined in the Agent SDK?

options.text: As an `AgentDefinition` with a description (used for selection), a system prompt, and a restricted tools list.
options.why: This is how the SDK defines specialised subagents.

options.text: As a paragraph in the coordinator's system prompt describing a fact-checker persona.
options.why: That gives no isolated context and no tool restriction.

options.text: As a separate MCP server.
options.why: MCP servers expose tools, not agent definitions.

options.text: As a CLAUDE.md file in the project.
options.why: That is memory, not an agent definition.

questions.explanation: `AgentDefinition` provides the description, system prompt and tool restrictions for subagents.

questions.stem: A client asks for a recurring monthly brief with the same fixed structure: market size, top 5 players, regulatory changes and outlook. Which workflow design fits best?

options.text: A prompt chain (or fixed pipeline) with known stages for each section, because the structure is stable and predictable.
options.why: Predictable, repeatable structures suit chaining.

options.text: Fully adaptive decomposition from scratch every month.
options.why: Adaptive decomposition adds variability that a fixed structure doesn't need.

options.text: A single prompt that writes the whole brief.
options.why: This loses focus, citations and validation between stages.

options.text: Ask the client to restate the structure each month.
options.why: This is unnecessary.

questions.explanation: Use fixed chaining for known structures and adaptive decomposition for open-ended discovery.

questions.stem: The synthesis agent receives prose summaries from subagents and loses track of which document each claim came from. Which TWO changes to subagent outputs help most? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Return findings as structured records (claim, evidence excerpt, source ID or URL, page or section).
options.why: Structured content preserves attribution across hops.

options.text: Include metadata such as publication date and source type with each finding.
options.why: Metadata supports provenance and recency judgements.

options.text: Return longer prose so more detail is preserved.
options.why: Length doesn't fix attribution.

options.text: Strip source references to save tokens.
options.why: This destroys provenance.

options.text: Have subagents write directly into the final report.
options.why: This bypasses the coordinator and synthesis.

questions.explanation: Pass structured content plus metadata between agents to preserve attribution.

questions.stem: The coordinator's context grows to more than 150k tokens because each subagent returns full fetched pages. Coordination quality drops in later steps. What is the best fix?

options.text: Have subagents return concise, structured findings (with source references) instead of raw pages, so the coordinator's context holds only what it needs to decide.
options.why: Subagents exist partly to absorb verbose work and return distilled results.

options.text: Give the coordinator a bigger context window.
options.why: It still suffers attention dilution and cost.

options.text: Have the coordinator summarise the pages itself.
options.why: The bloat has already entered its context.

options.text: Limit each subagent to one search.
options.why: This hurts research quality.

questions.explanation: Keep the coordinator's context lean: subagents return structured summaries with metadata, not raw dumps.

questions.stem: The `web_fetch` tool returns HTTP 403 for paywalled sites, and the search subagent keeps retrying them. How should the tool report this?

options.text: As an error with a permission or access category and `isRetryable: false`, so the agent moves on to alternative sources instead of retrying.
options.why: Categorised, non-retryable errors stop futile retries.

options.text: As an empty page with a success status.
options.why: This is an access failure masked as an empty result.

options.text: As a transient error, to encourage retries.
options.why: This is the wrong category and wastes calls.

options.text: By raising an exception that ends the research task.
options.why: This is disproportionate.

questions.explanation: Error categories plus retryability guide the agent's recovery: retry only transient failures.
